newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO police are poorly paid but highly motivated.
newsitem.headline: PLO police are poorly paid but highly motivated.

text.p: The PLO police who battled highly-trained Israeli troops in the West Bank and Gaza Strip last week won new respect among their people.
"We did not receive orders to fire at the Israelis and we did not wait for one. We acted out of our own will and because of what we saw," said one policeman, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

Young recruits, many inexperienced in warfare and short on ammunition, had intense gunfights with Israeli soldiers last week after Israel opened an archaeological tunnel in Old Jerusalem's Moslem Quarter.
In at least two incidents, the poorly paid Palestinians overran Israeli positions and gave stiff resistance to the better-equipped Israeli army.
"We could not bear seeing Israeli soldiers open fire on our people while we sit silently," said an officer in the Palestinian National Security Forces in Gaza.
Police were among 55 Palestinians killed during five days of violence. Palestinian forces killed 14 Israeli soldiers and paramilitary police. Scores were wounded.
An Israeli general termed a confrontation in which Palestinian rioters and police overran an Israeli position at Joseph's Tomb in Nablus in the West Bank "a real battle".
About 36,000 men and women serve in six branches of the Palestinian police, according to sources in the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which helps the Palestinian Authority prepare its budget.
Aside from regular police, Palestinians have a range of state security forces, paramilitary units trained in riot control, and the Force 17 unit to protect President Yasser Arafat.
Palestinian security forces, accused repeatedly of human rights abuses and corruption, had been used by Arafat to crack down on Islamic groups behind suicide bombings in Israel.

But last week's confrontations gained Palestinian forces new respect with their people, even as the sight of them firing at Israeli troops infuriated the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"We have people who can defend us! Go and get them!" shouted a woman outside Ramallah hospital as ambulances brought Palestinian casualties from the front lines.

At the core of Arafat's police are some 7,000 Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) guerrillas and Palestinian Liberation Army (PLA) soldiers who returned from exile in 1994 under an Israeli-PLO deal setting up Palestinian self-rule.
The Palestinian Authority has since recruited thousands of former activists who grew up during the 1987-1993 Palestinian revolt against Israeli rule.
Palestinian police officers receive a monthly salary of $260 after undergoing basic training at bases in the West Bank and Gaza, a security official said.

Palestinian police are allowed to carry light weapons under the self-rule accord with Israel. The deals also provided for a limited number of machineguns mounted on 45 armoured personnel carriers provided by Russia.
But the armaments are tightly controlled by Israel. Weapons brought from outside must be approved by Israeli officials, who keep an inventory of Palestinian guns and ammunition.
In last week's battles, Palestinian forces faced acute ammunition shortages. Policemen said they were issued only 30 bullets each.
